screens.title: Lighting, Materials & Post-Processing for 3D Realism
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will treat lighting, materials, and post-processing as a single visual toolset for realism. You will learn the practical purpose of each light type, why baked lighting is essential for static scenes, and how PBR materials respond to light through Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal and Occlusion maps. We also cover the Post-Processing Stack—Bloom, Ambient Occlusion, and Color Grading—and how to set it up on your camera. I’ll walk you through a short baking workflow and show a hybrid approach that uses light probes and a small number of real-time lights for dynamic objects. Along the way, we’ll surface common pitfalls, like overusing real-time lights or mismatching texture color spaces, and show how to avoid them. By the end, you’ll be able to bake static illumination, author PBR materials that read correctly across lighting, and apply post-processing effects thoughtfully so they enhance mood without hiding problems. Think of this chapter as a toolkit: practical steps, visual checks, and a performance-minded mindset to make your scenes both beautiful and playable.

screens.title: Light Types: Directional, Point, Spot, Area
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding light types is the foundation of scene lighting. Directional lights simulate a distant source like the sun; they send parallel rays across the entire scene so rotation matters but position does not. Point lights emit equally in all directions from a single point; think of a bare bulb whose influence falls off with distance. Spot lights project a cone, useful for flashlights or headlights where angle and range shape what the player sees. Area lights emit from a rectangular surface for soft, realistic illumination but are typically baked because they are expensive to calculate in real time. A concrete example: for an outdoor level you would use a Directional Light for the sun, a Point Light for a campfire, and a Spot Light for a torch beam the player carries. A common misconception is to use many real-time point lights for decorative bulbs; this often kills performance. Instead, bake those bulbs or use emissive materials and lightmaps. When choosing a light type, ask what must move or flicker, and what can be baked. That decision determines whether you need real-time shadows and whether probes or lightmaps are the efficient choice. How would you decide which single light must remain real-time in your scene?

keyIdea.text: Match light shape to physical source and to whether it needs to change at runtime; bake when possible.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Light Types
Definition

Common Unity light types

Each light type models a physical source and has trade-offs in range, shadowing, and performance.

Directional
Parallel rays, good for sun and global light. Rotation matters, position does not.
Point
Omnidirectional emission with distance falloff; ideal for bulbs and local lights.
Spot
Cone-shaped emission with angle and range controls; used for flashlights and focused beams.
Area
Rectangular emitters for soft light—typically baked due to cost.
Key Takeaway

Pick the light that models the physical source and scale its use by whether it must update at runtime.

Example & Common Mistake
Example: an outdoor scene uses a Directional Light for sun, Point Lights for lamps marked Baked, and a real-time Spot for a player flashlight. Common mistake: placing many small real-time point lights for decorative bulbs. This increases per-frame lighting cost and shadows. Instead, bake decorative bulbs into lightmaps or use emissive materials and a baked light for the overall glow.
Scenario
Indoor room with static lamps: mark lamps and walls Static and bake lights to get soft indirect bounces in lightmaps.
Check your understanding
If a light must flicker or move, it must be real-time. If it is purely decorative and static, prefer baking.

screens.title: Directional Light Deep Dive
screens.narratorSegment: Directional light is the simplest and most powerful global lighting tool in Unity. It simulates a distant source whose rays are effectively parallel across the scene. Because of that, the directional light’s position does not affect illumination; only its rotation matters. Use it to produce uniform sunlight with consistent shadows and global specular highlights on PBR materials. A concrete example: rotate the directional light to create long evening shadows, and you will immediately see changes across all static geometry without moving the light’s world position. A common misconception is to try and simulate multiple suns using many directional lights; this leads to unnatural doubling of shadows and unrealistic shading. Instead, layer additional local lights—points or spots—where you need variation. Directional lights are also commonly baked for static environments when you want high-quality indirect light and shadowing baked into lightmaps. The key practical check: if rotating the light changes every shadow but moving it does not, you are using a Directional Light correctly. How would you balance a directional sun and indoor area lights in the same scene? Directional Light Deep Dive means rotation defines sun direction and shadow angle; use it for global illumination and bake when possible for static scenes.. In practical terms, how global light behaves and why rotation matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Directional Light
Definition

Directional light behavior

Parallel rays, uniform illumination, rotation controls shadow angle, position ignored.

Visual effect
Creates consistent outdoor lighting and crisp shadows useful for sunlit scenes.
Practical tip
Rotate to change time of day. Do not rely on multiple directional lights to add contrast; use localized lights or post-processing for mood.
Key Takeaway

Directional lights are your global sun. Rotate for mood, bake for performance, and add local lights for variety.

Example & Misconception
Example: An outdoor plaza uses one Directional Light as the sun. Lamps around the plaza use baked Point Lights so they don’t add per-frame cost. Misconception: Multiple Directional Lights make the scene look brighter; in practice they create conflicting shadows and unrealistic lighting. Use localized lights instead for highlights.
Check
If shadow angles change when rotating, and position changes have no effect, the Directional Light is working as expected.

screens.title: Point vs Spot Lights: Local Illumination
screens.narratorSegment: Point and Spot lights are both local sources but they serve distinct purposes. Point lights emit in all directions from a single point and are best for lamps, bonfires, and small ambient sources. Their intensity falls off with distance, so placement and attenuation shape scene mood. Spot lights project a cone with angle and range controls, making them perfect for flashlights, searchlights, or any case where you want directional focus. A concrete example: in an indoor corridor use Point Lights to simulate ceiling bulbs and a Spot Light for the player’s handheld flashlight. The flashlight should remain real-time so it moves with the player, while ceiling bulbs can be baked to light static geometry. A frequent mistake is making both the flashlight and many ceiling bulbs real-time, which multiplies per-frame cost. Instead, bake decorative bulbs and keep only the moving spotlight real-time. Consider shadows: Spot lights can cast sharp directional shadows within their cone, which is useful for reading geometry detail. Which would you keep real-time in a crowded scene that must run on limited hardware? Point vs Spot Lights: Local Illumination means use point lights for omnidirectional fill and spot lights for directional focus; bake static local lights and keep moving sources real-time.. In practical terms, when to use omnidirectional light vs a focused cone. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Point vs Spot
Comparison
Point Light
Omnidirectional emission. Best for bulbs and small local sources. Intensity decreases with distance.
Spot Light
Cone-shaped emission. Controls angle and range. Ideal for flashlights and directional effects.
Practical placement
Place point lights near sources of ambient glow. Use spot lights sparingly where you need focused visibility or drama.
Example & Takeaway
Example: In a dungeon passage mark ceiling torches static and bake them as Point Lights. Keep the player torch as a real-time Spot Light to illuminate moving objects. Takeaway: match light permanence to real-time requirement.
Key Takeaway

Prefer baked points for static scene fill; use a single moving spot for interactive focus to preserve performance.

screens.title: Real-time vs Baked Lighting
screens.narratorSegment: Real-time and baked lighting solve different problems. Real-time lighting is computed every frame so it supports moving lights, animated shadows, and dynamic day-night cycles. It is flexible but computationally expensive, especially when many lights cast real-time shadows. Baked lighting precomputes illumination and shadows for static geometry and stores them in lightmaps, enabling complex indirect lighting such as bounces and soft color bleed at low runtime cost. A concrete scenario: mark a static room’s walls and props as Static, bake the main ambient lighting, and then add a real-time flickering torch for dynamic character interaction. The torch will affect dynamic objects and sample baked indirect light via Light Probes. A common mistake is making everything real-time for visual fidelity; this often reduces frame rate more than necessary. The hybrid approach is usually best: bake static environment lights and use a few carefully chosen real-time lights for interactive elements. When you inspect performance, baked lightmaps remove per-frame lighting cost for static meshes and let you allocate budget to dynamic effects where they matter most. How would you measure whether a light should be baked or real-time in your current project?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Real-time vs Baked
Define
Real-time lighting updates each frame and supports movement and animated effects. Baked lighting precomputes light interactions for static objects and stores results in lightmaps for runtime efficiency.
Pros of Real-time
Dynamic shadows and moving lights; required for flickering or mobile lights.
Pros of Baked
Complex indirect illumination, low per-frame cost, higher visual fidelity for static scenes.
Example & Guidance
Example: An interior level bakes room lighting and places Light Probes so moving characters sample indirect light. A torch on the player remains real-time and adds local shadows to dynamic objects. Guidance: bake everything that is static; reserve real-time lights for movement and interactivity.
Common mistake
Using too many real-time lights to try to achieve realism. Bake first, then add minimal real-time lights for behavior.
Key Takeaway

Pick baked for static geometry, real-time for dynamic elements. Use Light Probes to bridge the two.

screens.title: Light Baking Workflow in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Baking lights in Unity is a repeatable workflow that yields optimized static illumination. Start by identifying static geometry: walls, floors, and props that will not move. In the Inspector mark those objects as Static. Next open Window → Rendering → Lighting and confirm your Environment settings, including a Skybox if you want sky contributions. In the Lighting panel, switch to the Lightmaps or Scene tab and configure sampling quality and lightmap resolution reasonably for your target hardware. Set individual lights to Baked in their Inspector when they contribute to static illumination. Then click Generate Lighting. Unity will compute direct and indirect lighting, store results in lightmaps, and write them into your scene. As a concrete example, add a Point Light inside a room, mark it Baked, and regenerate lighting to see the baked shadow and soft bounce. Common pitfalls include forgetting to mark objects Static or using very high lightmap resolutions that blow up memory. Also, remember to place Light Probes where dynamic objects will move so they sample indirect lighting. After baking, test by toggling the Post-process Volume or camera settings to ensure the baked result matches your artistic intent. What small change would you make if your lightmaps look blotchy?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Light Baking Workflow
Step-by-step
  1. Mark static geometry as Static in the Inspector.
  2. Open Window → Rendering → Lighting and set Environment and Skybox.
  3. Set lights that will be baked to Baked in their light Inspector.
  4. Adjust lightmap resolution and sample settings for quality vs memory.
  5. Click Generate Lighting and inspect the resulting lightmaps.
Key Takeaway

Follow the baking cycle and adjust lightmap settings to tradeoff quality and memory for your target platform.

Concrete example
Create a small room, add floor and walls, mark them Static, add a Point Light set to Baked, then generate lighting. Observe baked shadows and indirect color bleed. If lightmaps look blotchy, increase samples or tweak lightmap resolution, but measure memory impact.
Common mistakes
Forgetting to mark Static and using extremely high lightmap resolution unnecessarily.
Pro tip
Place Light Probes to carry baked indirect light to dynamic characters and moving objects.

screens.title: Introduction to PBR Materials
screens.narratorSegment: Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, is a material model that aims to predict how surfaces react to light using a small set of physical parameters. The goal is consistent appearance across lighting environments. In Unity’s Standard Shader, core PBR inputs are Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal, and Occlusion. Albedo is the base color—the diffuse that defines broad color. Metallic identifies which parts of the surface behave like metal versus dielectric materials; metals reflect environment color differently than non-metals. Smoothness controls microfacet behavior: high smoothness yields sharp specular highlights, low smoothness scatters light for a matte look. Normal maps fake small bumps and grooves without more polygons. Occlusion maps add local self-shadowing in crevices. A concrete example: to make a polished robot, set Metallic close to 1 and Smoothness high; for a dungeon wall set Metallic to 0 and Smoothness low, then add a Normal map for stone texture. A common pitfall is using a Metallic map on a non-metal material or not configuring texture color spaces. The practical test: change lighting and watch how metallic and smoothness respond; PBR should maintain believable responses under different lights. What material would you tune first when moving a model from a bright outdoor scene to dim indoor lighting?

Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › PBR Materials
Definition

PBR in Unity

PBR aims for consistent, physically plausible material responses under different lighting conditions.

Albedo
Base color texture; set to sRGB color space.
Metallic
Defines metal vs non-metal behavior; metals reflect environment color.
Smoothness
Controls sharpness of specular reflections; high is glossy, low is matte.
Example
Robot (polished): Metallic near 1, Smoothness high, Albedo sets tint. Dungeon stone: Metallic 0, Smoothness low, Normal map for rough detail. Adjust maps and sliders to see immediate effect under your scene lights.
Common mistake
Using metallic values on inherently non-metal surfaces or importing textures in the wrong color space.
Key Takeaway

Tune Metallic and Smoothness first to define material family, then add Normal and Occlusion maps for detail.

screens.title: PBR Texture Maps: Albedo, Metallic & Smoothness
screens.narratorSegment: Texture maps are the primary inputs to PBR materials and each plays a distinct role. Albedo is the diffuse color and should be provided in sRGB so colors appear correct under lighting. The Metallic map can be a single channel or full texture that sets which areas behave like metal; white indicates metallic, black indicates non-metal. Smoothness controls microfacet variance: smooth areas create tight specular highlights, rough areas scatter and soften reflections. A concrete example: on a car shader you might use an Albedo map for paint color, a Metallic map to define chrome trim, and a Smoothness map to keep paint glossy while making tires rough. When importing textures, ensure Normal and Metallic maps are not treated as sRGB; they must remain linear so the shader interprets them correctly. A common pitfall is swapping texture import color spaces and seeing washed-out or overly sharp lighting. The practical test is simple: toggle Smoothness and observe specular highlight size, then toggle Metallic and observe how reflections pick up scene color. Which map would you prioritize when polishing a character’s armor? Map breakdown
Albedo
Base color; use sRGB so colors read under lighting.
Metallic
White is metal, black is non-metal. Controls reflection behavior.
Smoothness
High smoothness gives sharp highlights; low smoothness is rough and diffuse.
Practical example
Car paint: Albedo for color, Metallic to define chrome accents, Smoothness high for gloss. Character armor: boost Metallic for metal plates, use Smoothness maps to vary wear and polish. Import settings must match map roles to avoid incorrect shading.
Common mistake
Importing normal or metallic maps as sRGB color textures, which leads to wrong lighting interpretation.
Key Takeaway

Set texture color spaces correctly and iterate with lighting to tune metallic and smoothness for the intended material look.

screens.title: Normal and Occlusion Maps
screens.narratorSegment: Normal and Occlusion maps are powerful ways to add perceived surface complexity without increasing polygon count. A Normal map stores surface normal perturbations per pixel so the lighting solver sees bumps and grooves that do not exist in the mesh geometry. This is ideal for fine detail like screws, cracks, and brick mortar. An Occlusion map encodes ambient occlusion information that darkens crevices and corners to simulate small-scale shadowing where global indirect light cannot reach easily. A concrete example: a brick wall uses a Normal map to show mortar depth and an Occlusion map to deepen shadows between bricks. A common misconception is that Normal maps change silhouette; they don’t. Normals only affect shading, so edges still follow the mesh. If you need silhouette detail, you must add geometry or use parallax techniques. When authoring, keep Normal maps in linear space and ensure tangent space conventions match your pipeline. The closing check: if your Normal looks correct when you rotate a light but edges remain unchanged, your Normal map is working as intended. How might you use Occlusion maps and Light Probes together to improve character shading?

What they do
Normal maps perturb per-pixel normals to simulate bumps. Occlusion maps darken crevices to enhance perceived depth and contact shadows.
Normal map tips
Keep in linear space, ensure tangent-space convention matches engine, and remember normals do not alter silhouette.
Occlusion map tips
Use occlusion to darken crevices and combine with baked lighting or SSAO for richer shading.
Example
A dungeon wall: Normal map gives mortar depth; Occlusion map darkens gaps so corners read better when baked or under SSAO. Use Light Probes to carry indirect light to moving characters that interact with these shaded areas.

screens.title: Post-Processing Stack: Effects and Setup
screens.narratorSegment: Unity’s Post-Processing Stack applies full-screen image effects after rendering to simulate camera and film-like behavior. To set it up, install the package from the Package Manager. Then select your Main Camera and add a Post-process Layer component. Create a layer named PostProcessing and assign it to the camera’s layer setting so the component targets the correct volume. Next create an empty GameObject called PostProcessVolume and add a Post-process Volume component. Check Is Global for scene-wide effects and create a Post-process Profile asset to store effect settings. Add Ambient Occlusion, Bloom, and Color Grading to the profile and adjust intensities. Bloom makes bright areas bleed into surroundings and is useful for emissive materials or highlights. Ambient Occlusion adds subtle crevice darkening to enhance depth. Color Grading adjusts contrast, exposure, and saturation to set mood. A concrete workflow: toggle the volume on and off to compare before-and-after and avoid overuse. A common mistake is cranking Bloom and Color Grading high so they mask lighting or texture issues. Always tune post-processing to support the lighting and material work you already did, not to cover it up. Which effect would you toggle first to compare raw lighting versus enhanced look?

Ambient Occlusion
Adds subtle contact shadows in crevices to improve depth perception.

screens.title: Performance Optimization for Lighting & Rendering
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizing rendering is both strategic and iterative. Start by identifying static and dynamic content so you can bake what won’t change and reserve dynamic lights for interactive elements. Use Occlusion Culling to avoid rendering objects behind other objects, and rely on Frustum Culling which Unity performs automatically to skip objects outside the camera view. Implement Level of Detail, or LOD, to swap complex meshes for simpler ones at a distance and reduce polygon cost. Use Batching to combine many small meshes into fewer draw calls, which lowers C P U overhead. For lighting specifically, bake static lights, mark movable objects to sample baked indirect light via Light Probes, and limit the number of real-time shadow-casting lights. A concrete indoor scenario: bake primary room lighting, use Light Probes for the player and enemies, and keep a single flickering real-time Point Light for a torch. Common mistakes include over-baking with unnecessarily high resolution or failing to place probes where dynamic objects traverse. Always profile after changes to ensure that each optimization yields measurable benefit. What single optimization would you test first in your scene to see an immediate frame-rate improvement?

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will treat lighting, materials, and post-processing as a single visual toolset for realism. You will learn the practical purpose of each light type, why baked lighting is essential for static scenes, and how PBR materials respond to light through Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal and Occlusion maps. We also cover the Post-Processing Stack—Bloom, Ambient Occlusion, and Color Grading—and how to set it up on your camera. I’ll walk you through a short baking workflow and show a hybrid approach that uses light probes and a small number of real-time lights for dynamic objects. Along the way, we’ll surface common pitfalls, like overusing real-time lights or mismatching texture color spaces, and show how to avoid them. By the end, you’ll be able to bake static illumination, author PBR materials that read correctly across lighting, and apply post-processing effects thoughtfully so they enhance mood without hiding problems. Think of this chapter as a toolkit: practical steps, visual checks, and a performance-minded mindset to make your scenes both beautiful and playable.

Over the next screens you will develop practical skills to light a scene, author PBR materials, apply post-processing, and optimize rendering. First, you will identify and apply Directional, Point, Spot, and Area lights so you can build both outdoor and indoor lighting setups. Second, you will learn the difference between real-time and baked lighting and be able to bake lightmaps for static geometry to save runtime cost. Third, you will create and configure PBR materials using Albedo, Metallic, and Smoothness controls, understanding how those properties change an object's look under different illumination. Fourth, you will set up Unity’s Post-Processing Stack to add Bloom, Ambient Occlusion, and Color Grading, learning how each effect changes perceived depth and mood. Each objective is paired with a practical milestone so you can verify competency as you work through the hands-on activity.

These additional objectives focus on workflow details and performance strategies you will use in real projects. First, you will learn to place Light Probes so dynamic characters and moving objects sample baked indirect lighting correctly. Second, you will become comfortable configuring texture import settings so Albedo maps use sRGB while Normal and Metallic maps use linear space, avoiding common shading errors. Third, you will practice a full baking cycle: marking static geometry, generating lightmaps in the Lighting window, then inspecting results and adjusting samples. Finally, you will plan optimization steps—occlusion culling, frustum culling, LOD, and batching—to reduce draw calls and C P U overhead. Each card below contains a short mnemonic and a verified milestone so you can confirm the skill is working in your scene. Learning Objectives (continued) means concrete workflow and optimization skills let you ship realistic scenes that perform across platforms.. In practical terms, deeper skills and practical milestones. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding light types is the foundation of scene lighting. Directional lights simulate a distant source like the sun; they send parallel rays across the entire scene so rotation matters but position does not. Point lights emit equally in all directions from a single point; think of a bare bulb whose influence falls off with distance. Spot lights project a cone, useful for flashlights or headlights where angle and range shape what the player sees. Area lights emit from a rectangular surface for soft, realistic illumination but are typically baked because they are expensive to calculate in real time. A concrete example: for an outdoor level you would use a Directional Light for the sun, a Point Light for a campfire, and a Spot Light for a torch beam the player carries. A common misconception is to use many real-time point lights for decorative bulbs; this often kills performance. Instead, bake those bulbs or use emissive materials and lightmaps. When choosing a light type, ask what must move or flicker, and what can be baked. That decision determines whether you need real-time shadows and whether probes or lightmaps are the efficient choice. How would you decide which single light must remain real-time in your scene?

Directional light is the simplest and most powerful global lighting tool in Unity. It simulates a distant source whose rays are effectively parallel across the scene. Because of that, the directional light’s position does not affect illumination; only its rotation matters. Use it to produce uniform sunlight with consistent shadows and global specular highlights on PBR materials. A concrete example: rotate the directional light to create long evening shadows, and you will immediately see changes across all static geometry without moving the light’s world position. A common misconception is to try and simulate multiple suns using many directional lights; this leads to unnatural doubling of shadows and unrealistic shading. Instead, layer additional local lights—points or spots—where you need variation. Directional lights are also commonly baked for static environments when you want high-quality indirect light and shadowing baked into lightmaps. The key practical check: if rotating the light changes every shadow but moving it does not, you are using a Directional Light correctly. How would you balance a directional sun and indoor area lights in the same scene? Directional Light Deep Dive means rotation defines sun direction and shadow angle; use it for global illumination and bake when possible for static scenes.. In practical terms, how global light behaves and why rotation matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Point and Spot lights are both local sources but they serve distinct purposes. Point lights emit in all directions from a single point and are best for lamps, bonfires, and small ambient sources. Their intensity falls off with distance, so placement and attenuation shape scene mood. Spot lights project a cone with angle and range controls, making them perfect for flashlights, searchlights, or any case where you want directional focus. A concrete example: in an indoor corridor use Point Lights to simulate ceiling bulbs and a Spot Light for the player’s handheld flashlight. The flashlight should remain real-time so it moves with the player, while ceiling bulbs can be baked to light static geometry. A frequent mistake is making both the flashlight and many ceiling bulbs real-time, which multiplies per-frame cost. Instead, bake decorative bulbs and keep only the moving spotlight real-time. Consider shadows: Spot lights can cast sharp directional shadows within their cone, which is useful for reading geometry detail. Which would you keep real-time in a crowded scene that must run on limited hardware? Point vs Spot Lights: Local Illumination means use point lights for omnidirectional fill and spot lights for directional focus; bake static local lights and keep moving sources real-time.. In practical terms, when to use omnidirectional light vs a focused cone. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Real-time and baked lighting solve different problems. Real-time lighting is computed every frame so it supports moving lights, animated shadows, and dynamic day-night cycles. It is flexible but computationally expensive, especially when many lights cast real-time shadows. Baked lighting precomputes illumination and shadows for static geometry and stores them in lightmaps, enabling complex indirect lighting such as bounces and soft color bleed at low runtime cost. A concrete scenario: mark a static room’s walls and props as Static, bake the main ambient lighting, and then add a real-time flickering torch for dynamic character interaction. The torch will affect dynamic objects and sample baked indirect light via Light Probes. A common mistake is making everything real-time for visual fidelity; this often reduces frame rate more than necessary. The hybrid approach is usually best: bake static environment lights and use a few carefully chosen real-time lights for interactive elements. When you inspect performance, baked lightmaps remove per-frame lighting cost for static meshes and let you allocate budget to dynamic effects where they matter most. How would you measure whether a light should be baked or real-time in your current project?

Baking lights in Unity is a repeatable workflow that yields optimized static illumination. Start by identifying static geometry: walls, floors, and props that will not move. In the Inspector mark those objects as Static. Next open Window → Rendering → Lighting and confirm your Environment settings, including a Skybox if you want sky contributions. In the Lighting panel, switch to the Lightmaps or Scene tab and configure sampling quality and lightmap resolution reasonably for your target hardware. Set individual lights to Baked in their Inspector when they contribute to static illumination. Then click Generate Lighting. Unity will compute direct and indirect lighting, store results in lightmaps, and write them into your scene. As a concrete example, add a Point Light inside a room, mark it Baked, and regenerate lighting to see the baked shadow and soft bounce. Common pitfalls include forgetting to mark objects Static or using very high lightmap resolutions that blow up memory. Also, remember to place Light Probes where dynamic objects will move so they sample indirect lighting. After baking, test by toggling the Post-process Volume or camera settings to ensure the baked result matches your artistic intent. What small change would you make if your lightmaps look blotchy?

Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, is a material model that aims to predict how surfaces react to light using a small set of physical parameters. The goal is consistent appearance across lighting environments. In Unity’s Standard Shader, core PBR inputs are Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal, and Occlusion. Albedo is the base color—the diffuse that defines broad color. Metallic identifies which parts of the surface behave like metal versus dielectric materials; metals reflect environment color differently than non-metals. Smoothness controls microfacet behavior: high smoothness yields sharp specular highlights, low smoothness scatters light for a matte look. Normal maps fake small bumps and grooves without more polygons. Occlusion maps add local self-shadowing in crevices. A concrete example: to make a polished robot, set Metallic close to 1 and Smoothness high; for a dungeon wall set Metallic to 0 and Smoothness low, then add a Normal map for stone texture. A common pitfall is using a Metallic map on a non-metal material or not configuring texture color spaces. The practical test: change lighting and watch how metallic and smoothness respond; PBR should maintain believable responses under different lights. Normal and Occlusion maps are powerful ways to add perceived surface complexity without increasing polygon count. A Normal map stores surface normal perturbations per pixel so the lighting solver sees bumps and grooves that do not exist in the mesh geometry. This is ideal for fine detail like screws, cracks, and brick mortar. An Occlusion map encodes ambient occlusion information that darkens crevices and corners to simulate small-scale shadowing where global indirect light cannot reach easily. A concrete example: a brick wall uses a Normal map to show mortar depth and an Occlusion map to deepen shadows between bricks. A common misconception is that Normal maps change silhouette; they don’t. Normals only affect shading, so edges still follow the mesh. If you need silhouette detail, you must add geometry or use parallax techniques. When authoring, keep Normal maps in linear space and ensure tangent space conventions match your pipeline. The closing check: if your Normal looks correct when you rotate a light but edges remain unchanged, your Normal map is working as intended. Unity’s Post-Processing Stack applies full-screen image effects after rendering to simulate camera and film-like behavior. To set it up, install the package from the Package Manager. Color Grading adjusts contrast, exposure, and saturation to set mood. A concrete workflow: toggle the volume on and off to compare before-and-after and avoid overuse. Optimizing rendering is both strategic and iterative. Start by identifying static and dynamic content so you can bake what won’t change and reserve dynamic lights for interactive elements. Use Occlusion Culling to avoid rendering objects behind other objects, and rely on Frustum Culling which Unity performs automatically to skip objects outside the camera view. Implement Level of Detail, or LOD, to swap complex meshes for simpler ones at a distance and reduce polygon cost. Use Batching to combine many small meshes into fewer draw calls, which lowers C P U overhead. For lighting specifically, bake static lights, mark movable objects to sample baked indirect light via Light Probes, and limit the number of real-time shadow-casting lights. A concrete indoor scenario: bake primary room lighting, use Light Probes for the player and enemies, and keep a single flickering real-time Point Light for a torch. Common mistakes include over-baking with unnecessarily high resolution or failing to place probes where dynamic objects traverse. Third, use a hybrid lighting approach: bake static illumination to lightmaps, place Light Probes for dynamic objects, and reserve a small number of real-time lights for interactive behavior. Here are concise one-line reminders for rapid recall. Directional Light: simulates sun with parallel rays; rotation controls shadow angles. Point Light: omnidirectional source with falloff; good for bulbs. Spot Light: cone-shaped, controls angle and range for focused illumination. Area Light: rectangular soft source, usually baked because it is costly in real time. Real-time Lighting: recalculated every frame for dynamic changes but expensive. Baked Lighting: precomputed lightmaps for static geometry that offer complex indirect illumination at low runtime cost. Keep these short statements in mind while building and profiling scenes.
